content: Effective circulating volume (ECV) refers to the volume of arterial blood, which is the vascular extracellular fluid, that is actively involved in tissue perfusion. It is a dynamic concept and does not represent a measurable or distinct compartment within the body. In a 70 kg individual, the ECV is approximately 7 liters. This concept is particularly useful in understanding and discussing cardiovascular and renal physiology. While ECV typically varies in proportion to the total extracellular fluid volume, this relationship becomes disrupted in certain pathological conditions, such as congestive heart failure (CHF) or hepatic cirrhosis. In these diseases, a reduction in ECV can occur, which may trigger compensatory mechanisms associated with volume depletion, such as edema formation. A decrease in ECV can activate several physiological responses, including the stimulation of renin secretion, activation of the sympathetic nervous system, and the release of prostaglandins. These responses collectively help regulate renal blood flow and maintain the glomerular filtration rate, among other critical functions. Reference: John Bullock, Michael B. Wang, Joseph Boyle. NMS Physiology, Lippincott Williams & Wilkins, 2001, pp. 337-339.
